category_title: Disengaged male students at risk of dropping out with low self-esteem and preference for practical science
minimal_context: The student is working in a group to examine the chemical components of cigarette smoke and ash using a black filter and a highly prescriptive record sheet.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Today we are examining the chemical components of cigarette smoke. Please follow the exact steps on your record sheet to test the black filter and the cigarette ash.

STUDENT: Why do we have to follow this exactly? This is too prescriptive and rigid, and it's not giving us any room to plan or decide how to do the test.

TUTOR: Just read the instructions on the sheet and do what it says.

STUDENT: But this involves a larger amount of previous chemical knowledge. It is not easy to understand what we are even looking at.

TUTOR: Keep trying to get through the steps on the record sheet with your group.

STUDENT: I'm not doing this anymore. I don't enjoy this module because it doesn't make us think and it doesn't let us actually participate. We can't even deal with unexpected difficulties because it's too oriented.

options.A: Allow the student to keep the record sheet under the condition that they do not show it to their group members, and break off for lunch.
options.B: Use the 'bubble-blowing' technique to help the student visualize their thoughts about the prescriptive instructions and release them without judgment during the laboratory activity.
options.C: Adjust the pace of the lesson to give the student sufficient time to work over their difficulties and to explore deeply the studied chemical themes.
options.D: Encourage the student to listen carefully when a group member takes ownership of a particular chemical concept, directing them to talk to the new 'expert'.
